title: Mashed Potato with Milk and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato made from fresh potatoes, prepared with milk and cheese, is a smooth, creamy side dish. The potatoes are boiled until tender, then mashed and blended with milk and grated cheese, giving it a rich flavor and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the most widely consumed root vegetables worldwide, cultivated in over 100 countries.
The tradition of cooking mash with milk dates back to European cuisine of the 18th century.
Cheese not only enhances taste but also boosts calcium and protein content.
For an especially fluffy texture, the “Russet” variety, high in starch, is often preferred.
Mashed potatoes can be served on their own or used as a base for casseroles.

items.title: Source of Vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Rich in Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Contains Protein
items.content: Cheese adds complete protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium for Bones
items.content: Milk and cheese are good sources of calcium, contributing to bone strength.

items.title: Energy Supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from potatoes offer a quick source of energy.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from the milk and cheese.

items.title: High Sodium Content
items.content: Adding too much salt or using salty cheese can make the dish unsuitable for those with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy Allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk or cheese requires complete avoidance of this mash.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: Creamy mash with milk and cheese is relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Top with extra grated cheese, fresh herbs, or a pat of butter. For a lighter version, replace part of the milk with a plant‑based alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the mash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk to restore its creamy texture. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
